title: "2. Find the Technical Truth"
description: "Extract the technical model from architecture and documentation. Identify actors, resources, responsibilities, relationships, events, and state transitions."

## Overview

Before you can explain a system, you must understand it. This lesson teaches you
to extract the **technical truth** — the factual description of a system — from
architecture and documentation. You will produce a `concept.md` file that
captures everything the story must never contradict.

The technical model comes **first**, before any metaphor. This is the
foundational principle in action: we understand the model first, transform it
deliberately, and use story to make that understanding accessible.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- Identify actors, resources, responsibilities, relationships, events, and state
  transitions from architecture documentation.
- Write a `concept.md` file that captures the technical model of a system.
- Verify that the concept contains no metaphor or narrative imagery.
- Understand why the technical model must precede any storytelling work.

## The technical model comes first

It is tempting to start with a story idea. A restaurant! A detective agency! A
theatre! But if you start with the metaphor, you will smuggle in assumptions
about the system that may not be true, and you will leave out facts that
matter.

Instead, start with the architecture. Read the documentation. Draw the diagrams.
Identify who does what, what depends on what, and what happens when. Only when
you understand the model should you begin translating it into a story.

## What to extract

From any technical system, extract six categories of information:

| Category | Question | Example (Crossplane) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Actors** | Who participates? | Developer, Platform, Cloud Provider |
| **Resources** | What objects or entities exist? | XRD, XR, Composition, Managed Resource |
| **Responsibilities** | Who is accountable for what? | Provider realizes resources; Engine reconciles |
| **Relationships** | How do entities connect? | XR is matched to Composition; Composition generates MRs |
| **Events** | What moments matter? | Claim submitted, Composition selected, Reconciliation pass |
| **State transitions** | What changes from one state to another? | Desired vs observed; drift detected and corrected |

## The concept.md format

The output of this stage is a `concept.md` file. It has three parts:

1. **Plain-language model** — a step-by-step description of how the system works,
   in natural language, with no metaphor.
2. **Entities and responsibilities** — a table mapping each entity to its
   responsibility.
3. **Key facts the story must never contradict** — a list of hard constraints
   that any metaphor must respect.

::: {.callout-tip}
The concept must contain **no narrative imagery**. No restaurants, no characters,
no dialogue. It is the raw engineering truth. Metaphor comes in the next module.
:::

## Reference example

Read the complete Crossplane restaurant concept under
[`reference-example/concept.md`](../../reference-example/concept.md).

Notice how it:

- Describes the system in plain language first.
- Lists entities and responsibilities in a table.
- Specifies relationships as a tree.
- Identifies events and state transitions.
- States hard constraints that the story must never violate.

## The key facts rule

The last section of `concept.md` is the most important. It lists facts that the
story must **never contradict**. These are your safety net against metaphor drift
and misconception injection.

For example, in the Crossplane restaurant:

- The developer asks for a *composite* environment, not individual pieces.
- The XRD defines *what can be requested*; the Composition defines *how it is
  built*.
- The developer does **not** talk directly to providers.

If a metaphor would contradict any of these, the metaphor changes — not the
model.

## Common mistakes

- **Including narrative imagery.** If your concept.md mentions a restaurant, a
  character name, or a scene, you have gone too far. Strip it back to the
  engineering truth.
- **Omitting state transitions.** A story that only describes structure misses
  the dynamics. Make sure you capture what *happens* and *changes*.
- **Listing too much.** The concept should capture the model at the level of
  detail the story needs, not a complete technical reference. Focus on the
  entities and interactions the story will explain.
